name: verified-monitoring
narrative: Since the independent survey is what verifies the program, Maya can also inspect the quality of the survey itself — the focus shifts from reviewing program performance to reviewing the surveyors. Maya opens the independent survey's dashboard — the six-round trend. It confirms a real rise in independent survey-estimated coverage — 71.8%, against the 89.3% her program's own records report — with each round's confidence interval and sample size shown, so a change reads as real rather than sampling noise. Each round re-surveys a fresh representative household sample within the same matched ward pair, so the trend follows the same comparison over time. On the map, program delivery points fill only the intervention ward, but the survey covered both wards — so the gap between program-reported and survey-estimated coverage is real, not an artifact of where the survey looked. She toggles layers — service delivery, survey, the plan's sampled PSUs — showing where each looked. Maya checks the surveyors, one row each. The Connect app requires you to be within 15 meters to submit a survey, so everyone is 100% compliant — the quality signals are the photos, the on-primary rate, and the back-checks: a separate quality-control enumerator from the survey firm re-visited a random subset of each surveyor's households. One surveyor trips the quality threshold and is flagged. Maya opens that surveyor's back-check — the QC enumerator's re-visit against the original: sex, age, roof, location, vitamin-A result — and the answers don't match. Finally the Distributions table: the flagged surveyor's interviews ran impossibly fast and their roof-type answers collapse onto one value — statistical warning signs of possible fabrication that trigger further investigation, not a verdict. Everyone else varies normally. The flagged work is held for investigation and re-survey before it can count toward the coverage estimate — so a single bad surveyor can't quietly move the number.

maya.intro: Maya manages a Connect program delivering vitamin-A home visits. Her frontline workers log every visit through Connect and the coverage figure looks good — but Maya wants independent, drillable proof her program is actually reaching households and changing outcomes, not merely that visits were logged. And because the independent survey is what verifies the program, she also wants to inspect the quality of the survey itself: the survey's own per-surveyor quality and a back-check Maya can read row by row, including whether any one surveyor's data can be trusted.
maya.name: Maya Okafor

scenes.narrative: Maya's program looks good on paper — her workers log every vitamin-A visit, and the coverage number is high. But a logged visit isn't proof a household was reached, or that outcomes changed. So she commissioned an independent survey. And since the independent survey is what verifies the program, Maya can also inspect the quality of the survey itself — the focus shifts from reviewing program performance to reviewing the surveyors: the trend round over round, each surveyor's quality, and a back-check she can read row by row. Not 'trust us' — proof she can drill into.
scenes.title: The goal — independent, drillable proof the program works

features.description: A six-cycle line chart of the program self-report vs the independent intervention-arm survey vs the match-arm survey, with a shaded gap band, always-on 95% CI whiskers on both survey series, and a hover tooltip on every point (series, cycle, value, and for survey points the sample size + 95% CI).
features.verify: Assert three series render across six cycles; the legend reads Service delivery / Intervention survey / Match survey; the two survey series show per-round 95% CI whiskers; hovering a survey point shows a tooltip with the series, cycle, value, n and 95% CI; the latest round reads ~72% survey-estimated vs ~90% self-reported; no interpretive verbs on screen.

scenes.narrative: Maya opens the independent survey's six-round trend. It confirms a real rise in independent survey-estimated coverage — 71.8%, against the 89.3% her program's own records report — with each round's confidence interval and sample size shown, so a change reads as real rather than sampling noise. Each round re-surveys a fresh representative household sample within the same matched ward pair, so the trend follows the same comparison over time.
scenes.title: Six bi-monthly rounds over time — the gap holds

features.description: A full-width two-ward Mapbox map with a docked Layers panel (service delivery, independent survey, Plan · sampled PSUs, Work areas, Building footprints) drawn via the shared PlanLayers component; service-delivery points fill the intervention ward, every survey pin draws in both wards (each on a real sampled footprint, larger solid for the primary unit / smaller hollow ring for an alternate), and the map re-centres on a new real ward pair when the cycle changes.
features.verify: Assert both labelled ward boundaries and the Layers panel (delivery / survey / plan / work areas / building footprints) render; toggling Plan draws arm-coloured PSU hulls and does NOT recentre; clicking R1 then R6 re-centres the map on a different program/comparison ward pair.

scenes.narrative: On the map, program delivery points fill only the intervention ward, but the survey covered both wards — so the gap between program-reported and survey-estimated coverage is real, not an artifact of where the survey looked. Maya toggles the layers — service delivery, the survey, the plan's sampled PSUs — to see where each one looked.
scenes.title: Where delivery happened vs where the survey checked (the map moves)

features.description: A per-surveyor survey-quality scorecard (evidence, GPS, on-primary, completeness, duration, consistency, duplicates, back-check) computed per surveyor, with rose cells below threshold and a REVIEW tag on the flagged surveyor; the GPS column reads ~100% for all (app-gated) so the flag rests on the non-GPS signals; a consequence note under the table states that flagged work is held for investigation and re-survey before it counts toward the coverage estimate.
features.verify: Assert the table renders one row per surveyor with computed values, including an On-primary column and a ~100% GPS-within-15m column for every surveyor; exactly the flagged surveyor (T6) shows a REVIEW tag; its rose cells coincide with sub-threshold non-GPS values; a consequence note reading "held for investigation and re-survey" renders beneath the table.

scenes.narrative: Maya checks the surveyors, one row each. The Connect app requires you to be within 15 metres to submit, so everyone is 100% compliant on GPS — the quality signals are the photos, the on-primary rate, and the back-checks: a separate quality-control enumerator from the survey firm re-visited a random subset of each surveyor's households. One — T6 — trips the review threshold and is flagged, and flagged work is held for investigation and re-survey before it can count toward the coverage estimate.
scenes.title: The per-surveyor quality scorecard catches a surveyor

features.description: The flagged surveyor's back-check — Identity (sex / age / present / roof), Location (re-survey distance), Outcome (vitamin-A) agreement %s; two-row original-vs-re-survey rows; an info popup citing J-PAL/IPA + World Bank DIME.
features.verify: Assert the back-check renders for the flagged surveyor with Identity / Location / Outcome agreement %s; Identity includes a Roof column; the info popup cites dimewiki.worldbank.org/Back_Checks.

scenes.narrative: Maya opens T6's back-check — the quality-control enumerator's re-visit against the original: sex, age, roof, location, vitamin-A result — and the answers don't match.
scenes.title: The independent back-check confirms it

features.description: A per-surveyor Distributions (Layer-3) table — robust z-scores vs peers on dose yes-rate, interview speed, and answer-uniformity (roof-mix HHI), each as a raw-units lens (notch = value, bar width = |z|), plus a composite band — that surfaces the warning signs on speed + uniformity with no second field visit, framed as triggering investigation rather than a verdict.
features.verify: Assert the Distributions table renders one row per surveyor with z-scores on interview speed and answer uniformity; the flagged surveyor (T6) reads a red composite band with red speed + uniformity z-scores, while the other surveyors read green; the card copy frames these as warning signs of possible fabrication that trigger further investigation, not a verdict.

Everyone else varies normally. T6's work is held for investigation and re-survey before it can count toward the coverage estimate — so a single bad surveyor can't quietly move the number.
scenes.title: GPS is clean — the Distributions screen catches the fabrication
